analysis.one_liner: Gives people in managed care plans outside appeal rights, direct access to specialists, and the right to sue their health plan.
analysis.headline: The House passed the patients' bill of rights 275–151, with 68 Republicans joining 206 Democrats, but its text was attached to another bill and the Senate never voted on it before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set federal rules for managed care health plans: denied claims would get fast internal and outside review with binding results, patients could see OB-GYNs and specialists without gatekeeper referrals, emergency care would be covered without prior approval, and patients could sue their health plan in state court for injuries caused by coverage decisions. It passed the House with a large bipartisan majority, but its text was folded into a separate bill and it never got a vote in the Senate before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of people in employer-sponsored and insured health plans would gain: binding outside review of denied claims on fixed deadlines, emergency care covered without prior authorization under a "prudent layperson" standard, direct access to OB-GYNs and pediatricians and to specialists for serious conditions, protection of what doctors may tell patients, coverage of routine costs in approved clinical trials, and — for the first time under federal law — the right to sue a health plan in state court for personal injury or wrongful death caused by its coverage decisions [S2] [S4].

how_it_helps.text: Denials based on medical judgment could be appealed to an independent outside review entity, whose decision is binding on the plan, with penalties up to $1,000 a day for officials who refuse to comply.
Emergency care must be covered without prior authorization, using the 'prudent layperson' standard, and patients cannot be billed more than they would owe an in-network provider.
Patients get direct access to OB-GYN care, can designate a pediatrician for their child, and can receive standing referrals to a specialist for serious ongoing conditions.

The bill overrides ERISA's preemption of state-law suits, letting patients recover damages for personal injury or wrongful death caused by a plan's or insurer's coverage decisions — the first real legal recourse against HMOs.
Contracts that gag doctors from telling patients about treatment options are declared void, and doctors are protected for good-faith disclosures in the interest of quality care.
Plans must cover routine patient costs for people with serious illnesses joining approved clinical trials, and cannot penalize enrollment decisions for doing so.
Patients can be given the option of point-of-service coverage outside the plan's provider network.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and self-insured employers would bear the cost: they would have to run compliant internal and external appeals processes, cover emergency and specialty care on the bill's terms, offer point-of-service options, and — the most contested part — face state-court damage suits for injuries or deaths caused by coverage decisions. Employers could be sued only when they made the medical decision themselves. Some of the cost would likely flow to enrollees as higher premiums, and the bill's point-of-service option puts any extra premium on the enrollee unless the employer agrees to pay it [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The version the House passed added limits on lawsuits: it barred class actions for most of the bill's access protections and limited individual recovery to the benefits that were denied, leaving many patients without a meaningful remedy.
Punitive damages are barred in most cases once an external appeal has run and the plan has complied with its outcome, narrowing the deterrent effect of the new liability right.

The employer-liability carve-out is narrow — employers can be sued only when they exercised discretion to decide a claim themselves — but opponents argued the broader liability opening would drive up premiums and push employers to drop coverage.
The bill's point-of-service option puts any additional premium and cost sharing on the enrollee unless the employer agrees to pay it, so the choice of doctors comes at the patient's own expense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections were real and would have touched the health coverage of most working families: enforceable appeals, emergency care without pre-approval, and an end to gag clauses. The genuinely contested trade-off was the right to sue for damages, which insurers and employers argued would raise premiums, and the House-passed version had already been narrowed to bar class actions and cap remedies. The larger problem was not the design but the fate: a bill with a 275–151 bipartisan majority never received a Senate vote.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 275–151, but the rule that allowed the vote also attached its text to another bill and laid H.R. 2723 itself on the table; the Senate never took it up, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Charlie Norwood, a conservative Georgia Republican, introduced the bill with a bipartisan list of original cosponsors including John Dingell, and it drew 155 cosponsors in all — 132 Democrats and 23 Republicans.
The bill was referred to three committees — Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means — and never received a committee vote or report.

The House Rules Committee reported a rule (H. Res. 323) that considered H.R. 2723 alongside H.R. 2990, provided three hours of debate, and directed that once passed, H.R. 2723's text would be added to the end of H.R. 2990 and H.R. 2723 itself would be laid on the table.
On October 7, 1999, the House passed the bill 275–151, with 206 of 211 Democrats, 68 of 222 Republicans, and the lone Independent voting yes.
The House-passed version included limits on lawsuits: it barred class actions for many of the bill's access protections and restricted individual relief to the benefits that had been denied.
No further action was recorded on the bill; the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and self-insured employers were better off, since they never had to comply with the patient protections or face state-court damage suits for coverage decisions. Patients in managed care plans got no new federal rights from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: 206 of 211 House Democrats and 68 of 222 House Republicans voted yes, while 149 of 222 House Republicans voted no — bipartisan passage against a mostly Republican opposition.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care companies
industries.note: The bill would force insurers to follow binding external appeals decisions, cover emergency and specialty care on federal terms, and face state-court damage suits for coverage decisions that injure or kill patients. The industry fought the liability provisions, and its interest in stopping the bill ran directly against patients' interest in enforceable protections.

Self-insured employer plans are governed by ERISA, and the bill opened a narrow path to sue employers when they personally made the coverage decision that caused harm. Employers opposed the bill largely to avoid this exposure and added compliance costs.

The bill voids contract clauses that stop doctors from telling patients about treatment options, bars plans from penalizing physicians for patient advocacy, requires prompt payment of claims, and restricts physician incentive plans that reward denial of care.

By overriding ERISA preemption for personal injury and wrongful death suits against plans and issuers, the bill created a new class of state-court cases — one of the most contested provisions and a key reason opponents fought it.
